sentences.pattern: A sustainable choice is more likely to become routine when it is both + convenient + and + affordable.
sentences.cn: 当可持续选择同时具备两种实际品质时，它更可能成为日常习惯。

sentences.pattern: Having + tried a lower-impact option + once, a person may continue to + use it + if + the result is practical and visible.
sentences.cn: 在尝试过某种行为后，如果获得反馈，人们可能会继续行动。

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Sustainable habits spread when the better option is convenient.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Infrastructure and product design often influence household behaviour more reliably than moral appeals.
writingIdeas.argument: Most people make repeated choices under time and budget pressure rather than after detailed environmental research. If buses are infrequent or refill points are distant, good intentions are unlikely to survive a busy week. By contrast, convenient collection, reliable transport and efficient appliances turn lower-impact behaviour into the easiest routine. Individuals still make choices, but the environment shapes how costly those choices feel. Policy should therefore combine information with practical systems that make sustainable living ordinary.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Sustainable consumption can save money, but affordability is not automatic.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Environmental policies should distinguish between low-cost habits and investments that many households cannot make upfront.
writingIdeas.argument: Using leftovers or buying fewer clothes costs little and may immediately save money. Home insulation and efficient heating, however, require capital even though they reduce future bills. A tenant may also lack authority to improve the building while paying its energy costs. Grants, landlord standards and affordable finance can solve this mismatch more effectively than advising residents to spend wisely. Sustainable living becomes fairer when people can access long-term savings regardless of their initial resources.

speaking.question: Describe an environmentally friendly habit that fits easily into your life.
speaking.answer: The habit that fits most naturally is carrying a reusable water bottle. I began doing it mainly to avoid buying drinks while commuting, so the environmental benefit was not my only motivation. I leave the bottle beside my keys, which means I rarely forget it, and there are refill taps at my workplace. It saves a small amount of money and lets me see how much water I drink. I do not think this single habit has a dramatic effect, but it has lasted because it is convenient and useful. That has taught me that a sustainable routine is easier to maintain when it solves an everyday problem as well.

speaking.question: Do environmental labels help people live more sustainably?
speaking.answer: They can help when they compare products using clear and consistent criteria. A shopper cannot research every supply chain, so trustworthy labels reduce the effort required to make an informed decision. The problem is that vague claims such as “natural” or “green” may look official without explaining what was measured. Too many competing labels also create confusion. Independent standards, plain language and information about the whole product life cycle would make labels more useful, although price and availability will still shape the final choice.

reading.title: Why the Thermostat Display Changed Behaviour
paragraphs: A housing association installed smart energy displays in two hundred flats, expecting residents to respond to real-time information about electricity use. Early results were disappointing. People watched the figures for several days, switched appliances off more carefully and then stopped looking. Information had created curiosity, but it had not become part of household routine.

Researchers interviewing residents found that the display showed energy in technical units that meant little without comparison. A number rising from 0.4 to 0.8 kilowatts appeared important, yet users did not know whether it reflected a wasteful appliance or normal cooking. The device also reported immediate consumption, whereas monthly bills combined energy price, standing charges and previous use. Residents could not easily connect one careful evening with money saved.

The association redesigned the feedback rather than adding more advice. The screen compared each flat with its own previous week, identified unusually high overnight use and estimated cost over a month. It did not rank neighbours, since flats differed in size and occupancy. Most importantly, residents could set one modest target and receive a message when a routine—such as reducing standby use—produced a measurable change.

Six months later, average electricity use had fallen, although the distribution was uneven. Households with old electric heating had limited control over their largest expense, and some residents found repeated messages irritating. Those who saved most were not necessarily the people most concerned about climate change; they were often users who discovered a specific source of avoidable cost and could act on it without sacrificing comfort.

The trial does not show that every home needs another digital screen. It demonstrates that feedback supports sustainable behaviour only when people can interpret it, connect it to an available action and see a relevant result. A number, however accurate, rarely changes a routine by itself. Information becomes useful when it helps a household decide what to do next.
